item.title: Beyond the first transaction: Building inclusive digital payments for Bharat
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Sagar Kumar of PayU discussed how payment systems can improve accessibility, build user trust, and bring more consumers and small businesses into the digital economy.
item.content:encoded:
For digital payments to work for Bharat, getting someone to make their first transaction is only the beginning. The bigger challenge is making sure they feel confident enough to return, whether they are shopping online in their preferred language, making a payment independently, or running a small business.

At TechSparks 2026, Sagar Kumar, Vice President of Engineering at PayU, joined Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director – Strategic Content & Video at YourStory, for a fireside chat on the engineering behind inclusive digital payments.

Balancing speed with reliability

Having worked at early-stage startups and on systems handling millions of transactions, Kumar explained how engineering priorities change as businesses scale.

In the early stages, startup teams focus on speed, launching products quickly and learning as they go. But architecture remains important. Loosely coupled systems make it easier to add new business verticals without rebuilding everything from scratch.

At scale, speed is still important, but there is less room for error. Feature flags, incremental rollouts and A/B testing allow teams to introduce changes gradually, test them with specific customer groups and limit the impact of potential problems.

“Speed is the constant. It's just that the room for error will be smaller when you grow to a larger scale ecosystem, and in that process, you have to build enough safety nets,” he said.

Building for the next 100 payments

With UPI now familiar to many users in smaller cities and towns, Kumar believes the next step is to make online payments as intuitive as offline transactions.

PayU’s checkout pages default to a scan-and-pay option, offering an experience similar to what customers are used to at physical stores. The company has also launched Checkout for Bharat, which allows users to view checkout pages in multiple languages, making it easier for those who are less comfortable with English to complete payments.

But a simpler interface is only part of the solution.

For a first-time online shopper, seeing money debited from their account followed by a payment failure message can quickly undermine confidence. Kumar explained that payment systems need safeguards such as idempotency checks, which ensure that repeating the same request does not change the outcome after the first successful attempt.

These checks help prevent duplicate debits. Clear communication about failed transactions and automatic reversals are also important so customers do not have to initiate refund requests themselves.

“The next level of inclusivity, in my opinion, is not to bring a first-time user online to make payments, but to gain the confidence so that he makes another 100 payments. We engineer our systems to achieve that kind of a goal,” Kumar said.

Making accessibility part of engineering

In August, PayU launched an RBI-compliant checkout page designed to help blind and visually impaired users make payments independently.

The features include screen-reader voiceovers that identify important information such as payment amounts, merchant details, and transaction status. The company also made changes to button sizes, text layouts, and other visual elements.

PayU tested the checkout experience with blind and visually impaired users, who were able to complete payments independently rather than rely on someone else.

The company has also made accessibility part of its software development lifecycle, treating it as a consideration alongside functionality and performance when developing new features.

Kumar pointed out that these improvements can benefit other users too. High-contrast displays, for example, make it easier for delivery partners to view payment pages in bright sunlight. Clearly labelled interface elements can also help AI agents navigate checkout pages.

Keeping transactions running at scale

PayU processes close to 20 million transactions on an average day. At that volume, even a 0.1% failure rate could mean 20,000 unsuccessful payments.

Kumar explained that the challenge of operating at this scale comes from the number of systems involved. A single transaction can depend on merchants, issuing and acquiring banks, payment networks, aggregators, and multiple gateways. A slowdown or disruption in any one of these systems can affect the payment.

PayU uses intelligent routing to manage this complexity. Its systems monitor gateway success rates across several parameters, while machine-learning (ML) models help determine the best route for each transaction.

The algorithms also send a portion of transaction traffic through alternative routes to test their performance. This gives the system a real-time view of how different gateways are functioning.

If a gateway's performance deteriorates, transactions can be redirected to another option. Kumar said PayU has patented this routing algorithm.

The aim is to manage these complexities in the background so merchants and customers can complete transactions without having to deal with them.

Turning payments into business opportunities

Kumar also discussed how payment data can create opportunities beyond transactions.

UPI payments generate transaction histories that can help businesses understand customer payment behavior and support financial underwriting for specific credit needs.

PayU’s LazyPay addresses buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) use cases, while its merchant lending product helps small and medium businesses manage cash-flow requirements, including purchasing goods at more favourable prices. Repayments can be collected through daily settlements.

The company has also launched Agent HQ, which helps small businesses automate operational tasks such as following up with customers who abandon their websites, reconciling payments and initiating refunds.

By reducing the time founders spend on these activities, such tools can allow them to focus on growing their businesses.

For Kumar, the benefits extend beyond individual merchants. As small businesses grow, the wider digital payments ecosystem stands to gain too.

item.title: 5 lessons to learn from the book Kaizen by Sarah Harvey
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Kaizen by Sarah Harvey on building better habits, overcoming resistance, and achieving lasting personal growth.
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever decided to change your entire life, only to give up after a few days? Whether it is waking up early, exercising regularly, saving money, or learning a new skill, making major lifestyle changes can feel overwhelming. But what if you could transform your life without changing everything at once?

In Kaizen: The Japanese Method for Transforming Habits, One Small Step at a Time, Sarah Harvey introduces readers to the Japanese philosophy of Kaizen, which focuses on continuous improvement through small, manageable changes.

The book explains how this approach can be applied to different areas of life, including health, relationships, finances, career, and everyday habits. Instead of chasing overnight transformation, Harvey encourages readers to practise patience, understand their existing routines, and make gradual improvements that last.

5 Important lessons to learn from Kaizen by Sarah Harvey.

1. Small changes can lead to big results

One of the biggest lessons from the book is that you do not need to make dramatic changes to improve your life. Sometimes, the smallest actions can create meaningful progress when repeated consistently.

For example, if you want to develop a reading habit, start with just five pages a day instead of forcing yourself to finish an entire book in a week. Similarly, if you want to become physically active, begin with a short daily walk.

The idea is to make changes so manageable that you can continue them without feeling overwhelmed.

2. Understand your existing habits before changing them

Before introducing new habits, take some time to understand your current routine. Many people try to change their behaviour without identifying what is preventing them from making progress.

Harvey encourages readers to examine their everyday activities, identify areas that need improvement, and understand which habits are helping or holding them back.

For example, if you spend too much time scrolling through social media, observe when and why you reach for your phone. Once you understand the pattern, you can gradually replace that habit with something more productive.

3. Break big goals into smaller steps

Large goals can sometimes feel impossible because we focus too much on the final result rather than the actions required to achieve it.

The Kaizen approach encourages breaking ambitious goals into smaller, realistic tasks. Instead of worrying about writing an entire book, focus on writing one paragraph every day. If you want to save money, begin by setting aside a small amount regularly.

These manageable steps make it easier to stay motivated and track your progress.

4. Be patient and stop comparing your progress

Personal growth does not happen at the same speed for everyone. Some habits take weeks to develop, while others require months of consistent effort.

The book emphasises the importance of patience and creating solutions that suit your individual lifestyle. What works for someone else may not necessarily work for you.

Instead of comparing your progress with others, focus on becoming slightly better than you were yesterday. Remember that consistency matters more than perfection.

5. Track your progress and adjust your approach

Making changes is only one part of the process. You also need to understand whether those changes are working.

The book encourages readers to monitor their habits, review their progress, and make adjustments whenever necessary. Keeping a journal or maintaining a simple habit tracker can help you recognise improvements and identify areas that need more attention.

If a particular routine is not working, do not immediately consider it a failure. Find a more manageable approach and try again.

Final thoughts

Kaizen by Sarah Harvey offers a refreshing approach to personal development by reminding readers that meaningful transformation does not happen overnight. Instead of putting pressure on yourself to change everything at once, focus on making small improvements every day.

Whether you want to build healthier habits, improve your finances, strengthen relationships, or become more productive, the Kaizen philosophy encourages you to take one manageable step at a time.

The biggest takeaway is simple: you do not have to become a completely different person tomorrow. You just have to make a small effort to become better today.

item.title: From early traction to global scale: How AI is rewriting the cross-border playbook for Indian startups
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Manish Maheshwari from Stripe India stated that AI, local payments, and smarter cost control are accelerating global expansion for Indian startups.
item.content:encoded:
India has spent two decades getting good at building for Indians. The bigger opportunity now is building from India for everyone else.

That shift took center stage at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event, in a fireside chat titled ‘From early traction to global scale: Decoding cross-border commerce Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, India, Stripe, spoke with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, about what it takes to turn overseas sales into lasting growth.

A new way to build a company

Sharma opened by asking where India stands in the AI race. Maheshwari was optimistic. AI, he said, is creating a new way of operating, the minimum viable company, which “can be a one-person company”. For Indian entrepreneurs, that means they “can think global and go global on day one”.

Maheshwari backed this up with examples. Emergent, a startup out of India, reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR) in just eight months, while Pocket FM recently crossed half a billion dollars in ARR. Stripe Data shows that the number of companies collecting money from more than 100 countries has quadrupled in five years. For businesses earning cross-border revenue, ~25% earn most of their revenue outside the top 10 markets. .

Letting infrastructure do the heavy lifting

Sharma raised the worry on many founders’ minds: compliance. Maheshwari said a founder in Koramangala or Pune should focus on the core product, while a partner handles checkout, tax compliance, banking relationships, and money movement through a handful of APIs. Stripe, he said, was built around the idea of making money programmable, and “our heart beats for the founder”.

Physical goods work too. Maheshwari said 76% of customers prefer to pay in their local currency, and that offering local payment methods beyond cards lifts revenue by about 12%. He pointed to Purely Copper, a D2C brand that makes copper bottles in India, collects payments through Stripe, and ships to buyers in the US. Logistics, he noted, remains the seller’s job.

Keeping costs in check

The conversation then turned to Stripe’s agreement to acquire OpenRouter. Maheshwari explained that token costs are climbing, and at some new-age companies they now exceed salaries.

OpenRouter helps route each query to the right model in real time, balancing cost and latency, so teams do not use a frontier model for every task. Stripe already supports the revenue side through subscriptions, usage-based billing, and invoicing. With OpenRouter, it will help founders manage the cost side and the full P&L.

Where the next wave is headed

Looking ahead, Maheshwari said India rode the SaaS wave and the next one will be AI applications with global reach. 

“What you build in India could have customers in Brazil, could have customers in Colombia,” he said, adding that founders can find their ideal customer across dozens of countries at once. 

His message on location was simple: “You can sit in India and sell to the world.”

Getting started with Stripe

For founders keen to act, Maheshwari outlined three routes. Startups backed by top VC firms and accelerators receive Stripe credits by default; Stripe’s startup team engages directly with the ecosystem and runs knowledge sessions and webinars, and founders can also reach out through the website, though access in India is currently invite-only.

The audience questions that followed stayed on the same theme of reach. Asked about China, Maheshwari said Stripe supports Chinese payment methods such as WeChat Pay and surfaces local options based on a customer’s location and the business’s eligibility, with no local office needed for payments. Asked about AI agents making purchases on a user’s behalf, he said Stripe Link can automate payments within a limit and authorization set by the user, and that retailers are redesigning their websites to be machine-readable.

The road ahead

The session made one thing clear: the barriers that once kept Indian startups tied to the home market are coming down. AI is lowering the cost of building, payment infrastructure is handling the complexity of compliance and currencies, and new tools are helping founders keep spending in check as they scale. 

As Maheshwari put it, this is a great time to “think even bigger and think beyond India and think for the world”. For founders with a product that travels, the next step is no longer whether to go global, but how soon.

item.title: From multi-lingual AI agents to the future of voice: Google Cloud’s Naren Kachroo at TechSparks 2026
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Google Cloud’s Head of Sales & GTM AI showcased Gemini 3.8 Live and Live Avatar, and showed an AI sales agent negotiating a helmet order in Hindi on a weak mobile hotspot.
item.content:encoded:
For Naren Kachroo, the most useful AI is the kind that finishes the job. “There is no value created without the task actually getting completed with AI,” said Kachroo, Head of Sales & GTM AI at Google Cloud. At TechSparks 2026, during a product showcase titled ‘Voice AI in action’, Kachroo walked through Google’s latest voice models, customer use cases, and a live demo built for small businesses. His argument was: voice is becoming the main way people will interact with AI, and in India, that shift will happen in local languages and accents.

Kachroo said the industry has moved past treating generative AI as a question-and-answer tool. “We have moved from thinking about generative AI as chatbots, as something that we ask questions of and we get answers from,” he said.

The focus now is AI that has access to tools, data, and capabilities, and can take actions on a person’s behalf.

“We are not building AI for the sake of AI,” he added. The goal, he said, is AI that improves how people live and work everyday.

Two voice models, two jobs

Google recently announced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking. Gemini 3.8 Live can detect and switch between 97 supported languages within the same conversation. Kachroo explained how businesses should choose between the two models.

Gemini 3.8 Live suits simpler conversational and agentic tasks, such as a live voice chat with basic tool calling. Extended Thinking suits conversations that need deeper reasoning, context switching, and multiple steps. Cost also matters, he noted: Extended Thinking costs more per token.

Both are voice-to-voice models, which handle speech as input and output in a single model. For developers who need only one part of that pipeline, Google also offers separate models for text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and live translation.

Kachroo said the latest Gemini text-to-speech model performed strongly in Google’s internal testing with Indian languages, accents, and tonality.

What the demos showed

Kachroo played a series of short demos to show the range of use cases.

In the first, Shopify’s assistant, Sidekick, guided a merchant step by step through connecting a domain in the Shopify admin. In the second, a voice agent booked a restaurant table for eight people. Midway, the caller asked whether a cake was allowed, shared a photo from Google reviews to ask whether a dish was vegetarian, and asked about other vegetarian options before confirming.

The second demo required the agent to track context across multiple turns, remember preferences, and make several tool calls. That kind of task, Kachroo said, is where Extended Thinking fits.

He also showed Live Avatar, which pairs Gemini’s live voice with real-time video generation and lip-syncing, so users see an animated face as well as hear a voice. Google made Live Avatar available to businesses through Gemini Enterprise recently, and marks the audio and video it generates with an invisible SynthID watermark. Citi was a pilot customer: its Citi Sky assistant, built with Google DeepMind’s real-time avatar technology and the Gemini Live API, walks US wealth clients through options, such as what to do with a maturing certificate of deposit.

Why the cost is lower

Kachroo said Gemini 3.8 Live has the lowest cost per turn of any comparable model, and that Extended Thinking tops industry benchmarks for speech-to-speech quality.

Google has said Extended Thinking scored 82.6 on Artificial Analysis’ speech-to-speech quality index, the highest overall score.

The low price is not a land grab, he said. Google runs the full stack itself, from its TPU chips and infrastructure to the models and applications, and passes the efficiency gains on to customers. That lets Google offer both a top-quality model and a lower-cost workhorse model.

He pointed to two customers as examples of voice AI in use: Autotrader, which uses the technology for buying and selling used cars, and Equal AI, an Indian startup whose assistant answers and handles phone calls before the user picks up.

A sales agent for small businesses

The centerpiece of the session was a live demo of an assistant for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which Kachroo said his team built in about a day. It is a large potential market: more than 7.8 crore enterprises were registered on the government’s Udyam portal as of February 2026, according to the MSME ministry. Kachroo flagged one risk upfront: he was running it on a mobile hotspot after failing to connect to the hotel network.

The demo featured a fictional safety gear company and its owner, Rajesh, who had just received about 500 helmets. Speaking to the assistant, Rajesh asked how many leads he had for helmets. The assistant found two: a construction firm in Mumbai that needed 500 helmets, and a hardware store in Agra that needed 50.

Rajesh told the assistant to drop the smaller lead, send a quotation to the Mumbai buyer, and call them to close the deal. He set one condition: the price had to stay above Rs 400 per helmet, and the assistant could book the order without coming back for approval.

The assistant then called the buyer and negotiated in Hindi. Kachroo said it carried context from the internal conversation with Rajesh into the external call, negotiated on the company’s behalf, and closed the deal.

That end-to-end flow is where Google wants voice AI to go, he said. With the 3.8 Live models, he believes businesses can now build voice agents into their processes that complete tasks on their own.

Built for how India speaks

Kachroo said the assistant could have held the same conversation in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Kannada, Marathi, and other languages. That matters, he argued, because the Indian consumer is moving voice-first. Gemini Live itself now supports more than 25 Indian languages and dialects. According to the IAMAI-Kantar Internet in India 2024 report, 98% of India’s 886 million active internet users accessed content in Indic languages, and one in five used voice commands to go online.

“I believe that voice is the future,” he said. Voice AI in India, he added, will need to be native to the languages people speak, the accents they use, and what they are most comfortable with.

Kachroo said Google DeepMind has a team in Bengaluru researching voice, focused on Indian accents and cultural nuances. Google also funds Project Vaani, run by the Indian Institute of Science and ARTPARK, which has open-sourced more than 31,000 hours of speech in 105 languages from 165 districts.

Kachroo closed with an invitation for founders and developers to try the models, use the experiences, and share feedback, including what does not work, so that Google’s research and product teams can improve them. His larger point was that voice AI is ready to move beyond conversation into execution, and that India, with its range of languages and its voice-first users, is one of the markets where that shift will be tested first.

item.title: Gemini in action: How voice, agents, and coding tools are changing the way businesses use AI
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Google Cloud’s Rajesh Shewani walked through how businesses are using Gemini for voice, agents, and coding, and why the systems built around a model now matter as much as the model itself.
item.content:encoded:
Generative AI, in the form most people know it, is only about three years old. In that short time, Rajesh Shewani believes it has already moved through three distinct eras.

First came retrieval: chatbots that answer a question and wait for the next one. Then came agents that take action on a user’s behalf. Now, he said, the industry is entering what he calls the harness era, where orchestration, memory, and guardrails around a model let it carry out work from start to finish.

“An agent is nothing now but a model plus a harness,” said Shewani, Head of AI Customer Engineering for Digital Natives, Startups and ITeS at Google Cloud, at TechSparks 2026.

In a masterclass titled ‘Gemini in action’, Shewani promised a look at what is happening rather than a sales pitch. He covered where businesses are putting AI to work, how voice is becoming an interface, the tools Google uses to build its own software, and the questions organisations need to answer as agents become everyday users of their systems.

Shewani said organizations are no longer just discussing AI but executing in five broad areas.

  1. Agents, which are changing how companies work and how startups build for other businesses.
  2. Creative work, from image and video generation to marketing and branding, was one of the earliest areas to take off.
  3. Multimodal AI, which lets models work with images, video, and voice, not just text.
  4. Physical AI, including robotics and self-driving cars, which he expects to grow fast as the “brain” of large language models gains a body.
  5. AI fluency, a priority for traditional organizations in banking, insurance, retail, and telecom.

For those traditional businesses, the worry is less about building models and more about whether employees can use AI in their daily jobs. They don’t need to be experts or developers, he said, but they do need to be fluent.

What every agent needs

The three eras are cumulative, Shewani explained. Agents build on retrieval, and harnesses build on agents. AI is no longer an assistant that appears and disappears, but something closer to an autonomous colleague.

“It’s no longer just about the model,” he said. “It’s the model plus everything that you build around it”, from memory and context management to sandboxing.

He described four things every agent needs:

  • A goal: booking a ticket, making an entry in an SAP system, or negotiating a price by voice.
  • Instructions: guidance that goes beyond a single prompt and can be stored for reuse, much as new employees learn how an organization works.
  • Knowledge: a company’s own data, since models are trained on public information, not internal records.
  • Tools: the means to act, such as updating a CRM or placing an outbound call.

Knowledge is where much of the effort is going. Many teams had begun building their own “LLM wikis” for agents, and Google is now trying to standardize the approach with the Open Knowledge Format (OKF). OKF v0.1 represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, which agents can read directly. Shewani compared its role to what Model Context Protocol (MCP) did for backend integration.

A shared knowledge layer, combining a knowledge graph with plain text, also keeps costs down, he said. Rather than querying everything for every prompt, agents are pointed to structured context, which uses fewer tokens.

Voice becomes the interface

“Voice is becoming the new user interface,” Shewani said, whether for customers, employees, or users who prefer to speak in local languages. He noted that Google DeepMind’s team in Bengaluru is doing extensive work on Indic languages. Gemini Live now supports more than 90 Indian languages and dialects, including Sanskrit, Bhojpuri, and Maithili.

He showed a live translation demo built for Grab, the Southeast Asian ride-hailing platform, in which a passenger and driver who do not share a language coordinate a pickup.

Grab says travellers and driver-partners make more than 10 million voice calls a month, and it has been testing Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, which offers two-way translation in more than 70 languages.

Shewani said Gemini 3.8 Live, launched in September, improves further on noise cancellation and conversations between multiple speakers.

Another demo, built in India, dubbed a news video into Marathi and Malayalam from a single prompt while matching lip movements and facial expressions. Dubbing once required complex pipelines with many steps, he said, but live models have cut those down significantly, making it easier to create training videos and marketing content across languages.

He also showed Citi Sky, Citi’s AI-powered wealth assistant, which uses a virtual avatar to walk clients through options for a maturing certificate of deposit and complete the renewal. For such experiences, latency is critical. “If a flow breaks even for a second or a millisecond, it doesn’t work,” he said.

The stack under the hood

Shewani then walked through the tools that sit beneath these experiences.

Gemini agent is a single agent that can carry out tasks end to end. Google Cloud introduced it on October 8, 2026, and it can keep working in the cloud for hours or days, even when a user’s device is offline.

Shewani gave the example of a procurement team asking it to research options, write a request for proposal, send it to vendors, evaluate responses, and produce a shortlist. According to Google, the agent routes each task to the most suitable model, currently choosing between Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude models.

Gemini Enterprise adds guardrails and quotas for businesses, which Shewani said helps keep costs from running away, a key concern in tokenomics. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian has said nearly 90% of Fortune 100 companies use Gemini Enterprise.

Antigravity is Google’s harness for building software, available as a command-line tool and as extensions for code editors. Shewani said most of Google’s own code is now written using the same harness, known internally as Jetski. Google CEO Sundar Pichai has said 75% of new code at Google is now generated by AI and reviewed by engineers, up from 25% in October 2024.

CodeMender scans code for vulnerabilities, creates patches, tests them in a sandbox, and can integrate with a GitHub repository. When Google DeepMind first announced it in October 2025, it had already contributed 72 security fixes to open-source projects.

Google is also giving every agent its own identity, which Shewani likened to an LDAP directory for agents, so organisations can track which agent took which action.

Choosing the right model for the job

No model can be cheapest, fastest, and most capable at once, Shewani said, so businesses need a range of models and should match each task to the right one. Google’s Flash models are its workhorses for everyday tasks that do not need complex reasoning.

“If I need to get to office every day, I don’t need to have a Ferrari,” he said. For the hardest work, there is Gemini 4 Argon.

Google made Gemini 4 Argon, its latest frontier model, generally available on October 13, 2026, at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens 95% cheaper. Google says it ranks first on the Vals Index, and Shewani pointed to software engineering, cybersecurity, and knowledge work in finance, legal, HR, and procurement as its main use cases.

He showed two examples. In one, Argon processed more than 80,000 raw files from NASA’s open archive, including CSVs, images, PDFs, logs, and videos, and turned the analysis into a presentation that followed a custom slide template. In another, it wrote more than 5,000 lines of Python to render a photorealistic 3D library interior from scratch, with no graphics libraries or rendering engine.

Argon can also generate up to one million output tokens, not just accept one million as input. Shewani said this helps with tasks such as mathematical proofs and multi-file code generation, where producing one large output instead of many small ones uses fewer tokens and runs faster.

Questions every organization should ask

Shewani closed with the questions businesses need to start answering now that agents are here. Will agents become the primary users of their systems? Are their databases ready for swarms of agents firing queries that no person wrote? How will they manage agents that do things they are not allowed to do?

Roles will change too. “Developers are essentially going to become managers of agents,” he said. Organizations will also need to manage budgets, route tasks across a mix of models, track telemetry and memory, and prepare for agents that generate their own user interfaces.

Asked about education, he said agents are already being used to create content in multiple languages, build AI tutors, generate quizzes, and grade students. Google offers such tools through Google for Education, he noted, and many edtech companies are building their own. In education, he added, avoiding hallucination is critical, which is why grounding agents in a trusted knowledge repository matters.

For Shewani, the shift is clear. The competition between models will continue, but the advantage increasingly lies in what businesses build around them: the knowledge they give agents, the guardrails they set, and the systems ready to work alongside them.

item.title: 5 lessons to learn from The Secret by Rhonda Byrne
item.description: Discover five life-changing lessons from The Secret by Rhonda Byrne on positive thinking, gratitude, visualisation, belief, and the law of attraction.
item.content:encoded:
What if the way you think about your life influences the way you experience it? Our thoughts, beliefs, and expectations can shape our decisions, actions, and outlook towards the future. Learning to direct them towards what we want can help us approach life with greater confidence and purpose.

In The Secret, Rhonda Byrne introduces readers to the law of attraction, a philosophy based on the idea that positive thoughts attract positive experiences, while negative thoughts attract negative ones. The book encourages readers to focus on their desires, practise gratitude, and visualise the life they want to create.

While positive thinking alone cannot guarantee specific outcomes, the book offers interesting lessons about mindset, self-belief, and intentional living.

5 Important lessons to learn from The Secret by Rhonda Byrne

1. Your thoughts influence your reality

One of the central ideas in The Secret is the law of attraction. According to this principle, the thoughts and feelings you focus on influence the experiences you attract into your life.

When you constantly focus on fear, failure, and limitations, you may find it harder to recognise opportunities. On the other hand, developing a positive outlook can help you approach challenges with greater confidence.

The lesson is to become more conscious of your thoughts and focus on possibilities rather than constantly expecting the worst.

2. Practise gratitude every day

Gratitude is one of the most important practices discussed in the book. Instead of focusing only on what you lack, learn to appreciate what you already have.

Whether it is your health, family, friendships, career, or small everyday moments, recognising the good things in your life can change your perspective.

The book encourages readers to make gratitude a daily habit. You can begin by writing down three things you are thankful for every morning or before going to bed.

3. Visualise what you want to achieve

The book introduces visualisation as a way to develop a clearer picture of your desired future.

Imagine achieving your goals, building the career you want, travelling to your dream destination, or becoming more confident. Try to picture the experience and the feelings associated with it.

Visualisation can help you clarify your priorities and stay motivated. However, it should be accompanied by practical planning and consistent action to turn your goals into reality.

4. Believe that you deserve good things

Self-belief plays an important role in how we approach opportunities and challenges. Sometimes, we hold ourselves back because we feel unworthy of success, happiness, or meaningful relationships.

The Secret encourages readers to develop positive beliefs about themselves and become more open to receiving good things in life.

Instead of constantly questioning whether you are capable, start recognising your strengths and working towards the opportunities you want.

5. Focus on what you want, not what you fear

Another important lesson from the book is to direct your attention towards the things you want to experience rather than constantly thinking about what you want to avoid.

For example, instead of repeatedly telling yourself that you do not want to fail, focus on what success would look like and what steps you can take to achieve it.

Changing the direction of your attention can help you develop a more constructive mindset and make decisions that support your goals.

Final thoughts

The Secret by Rhonda Byrne encourages readers to become more mindful of their thoughts, practise gratitude, and develop a positive outlook towards life.

Although the law of attraction is a philosophical concept rather than a scientifically established law, the book's emphasis on self-belief, visualisation, and intentional thinking can inspire readers to reflect on their goals. Its biggest takeaway is simple: focus on the life you want to build, appreciate what you already have, and take meaningful steps towards becoming the person you aspire to be.

item.title: Mangaluru’s Zupple Labs wins DRDO’s first-ever blockchain defence project
item.description: DRDO has picked Mangaluru’s Zupple Labs under its TDF to build India’s first security-audit framework for defence blockchain apps.
item.content:encoded:
Mangaluru-based Zupple Labs has been selected by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) under its Technology Development Fund (TDF) programme. Its brief: build India's first indigenous framework for security auditing of blockchain applications in the defence sector.

The selection is rare by any measure. Fewer than 90 projects have made it through the TDF programme in its ten-year history, and this is the first in the blockchain domain.

What DRDO has asked Zupple Labs to build

Over the next 30 months, Zupple Labs will develop a platform that DRDO will use to standardise security audits of upcoming blockchain applications across the defence sector.

As defence agencies explore distributed ledgers for records, logistics and authentication, a common auditing standard matters. It gives every new application the same security bar before deployment, and keeps that capability built and owned in India.

Trust infrastructure for governments

Zupple Labs builds blockchain-powered trust infrastructure for governments and institutions, with a presence across four countries. Its systems secure and authenticate critical citizen records, making them tamper-evident and verifiable.

The records it handles include:

  • Land records
  • Educational credentials
  • Identities
  • Permits and work orders

A client list that spans continents

The DRDO mandate builds on an established public-sector track record. Zupple Labs has delivered solutions for:

  • The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
  • The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA)
  • The Australian and New Zealand student immigration ecosystems
  • The Governments of Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra
  • The Government of Kenya

Work with national ministries, a UN agency and foreign governments gives the startup experience in exactly the kind of high-stakes, compliance-heavy environments that defence demands.

From Mangaluru to the national stage

Zupple Labs was a winner of the Karnataka government's Elevate programme in 2019. Seven years on, its DRDO selection is a strong signal for the state's Beyond Bengaluru push to grow startup hubs outside the capital.

Congratulating Zupple Labs on securing a project under DRDO’s TDF programme, Capt Brijesh Chowta, Member of Parliament from Dakshina Kannada, said: “Glad to see Zupple Labs, one of the 10 start-ups in this year’s ‘Bolpu’ cohort, making strides in strengthening the security and resilience of blockchain technology and contributing to India’s growing cybersecurity capabilities.”

The point goes beyond one company. Deep-tech work of national significance is now coming out of Karnataka's tier-2 cities, and Mangaluru is proving it can build for governments, global institutions and the country's defence establishment.

item.title: Global by default, local by design: What Indian founders learned about scaling across borders
item.description: At a Stripe roundtable at TechSparks 2026, leaders from edtech, commerce, fintech, and consumer hardware shared how to pick markets, localize smartly, and build the payments and compliance spine that makes expansion repeatable
item.content:encoded:
For many Indian businesses, going global does not begin with a grand strategy. It begins with a signup from a shopper in Texas, a lead from Dubai that lands at 2 a.m., or a customer in London who wants to pay in pounds. The first sale feels like proof. The harder question is whether the next market will follow the same path or demand starting from scratch. That question anchored a roundtable by Stripe on building a repeatable global growth playbook at TechSparks 2026, YourStory’s flagship event. 

The table brought together leaders from organisations like Xoxoday, upGrad, Dodo Payments, Bhanzu, Borderless Access, Cuemath, FreshtoHome, Codingal, Codeyoung and Ultrahuman.

Representing the host was Manish Maheshwari, Managing Director, India, Stripe. The conversation was moderated by Madanmohan Rao, Research Director, YourStory.

Prove demand before crossing borders

The discussion opened with a shared instinct: start small and start by listening. Companies weigh customer acquisition cost, lifetime value, and operational scalability, along with whether reliable payment rails and local talent exist. One approach was to collect leads and call them before a product even existed, since online research rarely surfaces micro-level insight. A market that keeps asking for the same thing earns a place on the roadmap, while a single large client in one location is better treated as a customization. The first paying customer proves little, while repeat purchases and low dispute rates tell the real story.

Localize the edges, standardize the core 

Anything that touches the end user, such as catalogs, curriculum and preferred payment modes like ACH in the United States or direct debit in the United Kingdom, can flex by market. Anything that moves money, including core fraud rules, stays standard. Legal and regulatory needs come first, followed by customer-specific requests, whether that means a bright red palette in China or tax-inclusive pricing in India. Pricing deserves equal care, as carrying Indian price points into the US took one team a long time to correct. Partnerships help too. In the UAE, a government tie-up won acceptance for credentials, while local payment partners improved affordability and brought in new customers.

Treat payments as a growth lever

Maheshwari offered a caution that resonated across the table: “Your payment failure or your checkout failure can be mistaken as a demand failure.” 

Pricing in local currency is a big part of the fix, with Stripe’s data showing that 76% of customers prefer to pay in their own currency. Local payment methods and installments for large purchases help, as does a stack that is standard at the core but adaptable by country. Fraud control is a balancing act, because tightening rules too far turns away genuine buyers. Tracking chargebacks, refunds and failure rates by country also helps teams find leaks, such as overseas customers whose one-time passwords never arrived under Indian authentication rules.

Make compliance part of the product

Revenue brings obligations. US states set their own tax thresholds, Europe and India have data rules, and even text messaging follows different regulations in each country. Notices and penalties tend to arrive just as growth does, and one founder recalled how an India-only business shrank overnight after a regulatory shock. Stripe’s view was that a global stack chosen on day one costs less, since “going back and fixing it is far more expensive”. 

Tools such as Stripe Atlas, helps businesses create a US entity,, set up local banking, accept payments and raise funds early in their journey, before international growth makes those decisions harder to revisit. 

Let AI speed things up, with guardrails

AI is already compressing timelines. Content localization has become nearly 4X faster, with human verification and evaluation layers still in place, and engineers increasingly act as reviewers of AI-written code. Sales bots handle lead qualification and reminders across time zones, lifting funnel performance by an estimated 20-25%. Speed, however, raises questions of stability, safety and security, and cybersecurity was flagged as the topic most missing from the conversation.

Plant the flag where the pull is

Being global by default does not mean opening offices everywhere. One team that localized its curriculum and hired instructors and sales staff in Japan saw momentum fade within three months, because the effort amounted to a separate business. The lesson was to scale where strengths already exist, go deep, and then widen. 

Audiences beyond the Indian diaspora need a different approach altogether, with local hiring, community events and even offline centers in the US to feel like a native brand.

A playbook still taking shape

Taken together, the repeatable playbook is clear: validate repeat demand, keep the money-moving core standard, localize what customers see, build finance and compliance muscle early, and enter markets where pull already exists. 

Gaps remain. Paying individuals abroad, such as teachers, from an Indian entity is still expensive, and the infrastructure for it is thin. 

As the evening closed, the shared belief was that the best learning comes from peers who work in the field. For Indian businesses, going global market by market is less a leap than a discipline, built one repeatable decision at a time.

item.title: Keralam positions itself as a value-driven launchpad for deeptech startups
item.description: The Keralam government is keen to enhance the value of its startup ecosystem especially with the deeptech segment providing financial and other infrastructure support
item.content:encoded:
Keralam wants to build its startup ecosystem and lead from the front, especially in deeptech and AI.

At the inaugural of Huddle Global 2026, a beachside startup festival of the Keralam government, Chief Minister V D Satheesan said, “Our next task is to take Kerala's companies to the world. Kerala does not need the most startups. It must be the place where startups grow stronger.”

The state which had about 300 startups in 2016 now has around 9,200 such young companies with a combined valuation of $1.7 billion. The startup segment of Keralam has attracted over Rs 8,500 crore of funding.

Huddle Global has been positioned by the Keralam government as a showcase of its startup ecosystem and the inaugural edition was held in 2018.

The chief minister said there will be a shift in its approach for its startup ecosystem where the first phase was all about a mission and the second phase is to scale this mission.

He also highlighted that the state government has been supporting the startups through a fund of funds programme and is looking to strengthen this initiative by increasing the limits of its innovation grants, R&D support and seed funding.

“Our aim is simple. In Kerala, a good idea should never fail for the lack of capital,” Satheesan remarked.

The Chief Minister also stressed on the role of future technologies coming into play and the State government is looking to strengthen its incubation network through stronger partnerships with academia.

P K Kunhalikutty, Minister for Industries, IT, Future Technology and Startups, Keralam said, “Our focus will also be on emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence.” He further added that the government will bring in more initiatives in this segment to attract investments.

“Kerala is entering an important phase of economic transformation. We are focusing on attracting domestic and international investment, promoting emerging industries and creating new opportunities for sustainable growth,” the minister said.

S Suhas, Special Secretary, Electronics and IT Department, government of Keralam, highlighted the progress made by the startup ecosystem in the State. This includes building an edge AI chip, a satellite launch along with SpaceX, a mechanical manhole cleaning machine that has bagged in contract in Singapore etc.

“In Keralam one no longer has to ask whether it can build startups. The question today is how big they can grow,” he remarked.

The official said the government has taken numerous steps to encourage the startups in the State, especially becoming the first customers for these young companies.

He also stressed the growth of innovation centres in Keralam with over 600 colleges having such facilities with 63 incubators and over 10 lakh square feet of startup space.

The target of the Keralam government is to have around 100 deeptech startups valued at Rs 100 core and above.

item.title: Jensen Huang resigns after 33 years at Nvidia
item.description: Nvidia has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive officer and board member with immediate effect, ending his 33-year tenure as the company’s chief executive, following a turbulent week.

Nvidia has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive officer. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent successor.

Kress said, “Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”

Kress will retain the finance role while serving as interim CEO. She joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft.

The board appointed former Synopsys chief executive and executive chairman Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever chair. 

Jones said Kress understood the business and its customers. He added, “The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”

On November 8, Huang apologised in a company-published message for being unfaithful to his wife and pledged to co-operate with an independent board inquiry into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.

Reports say Huang had another extramarital affair with a senior executive of Nvidia, in addition to the relationship with a Chinese national Alice Huang, who was allegedly recruited as an intelligence asset by the Chinese government.

On November 10, independent directors appointed former acting US attorney Joon H. Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the inquiry. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or company information had been compromised.

Nvidia faces a fast-growing, increasingly competitive AI-chip market. Founded in 1993 as a graphics-chip maker, it later adapted GPUs for parallel computing through software such as CUDA. 

In its latest reported quarter, ended on July 26, it recorded revenue of $96.2 billion, including $89 billion from data centres. Its next results are due on November 17.

item.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (November 12, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Thursday, November 12, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
From Jensen Huang's position as the CEO of Nvidia, to why Vikas Malpani thought he would feel like he had won when Quikr bought CommonFloor in 2016, here are the latest developments across sectors.

Featured Stories

Nvidia board to meet to decide CEO Jensen Huang's future at the company

Jensen Huang's position as the CEO of Nvidia looks increasingly uncertain with new details of extra-marital affairs emerging. The board is meeting soon to decide whether to oust him from the company he co-founded in 1993, according to reports.

Reports say Jensen had another extramarital affair with a senior executive of Nvidia. This is in addition to the relationship he had with a Chinese national Alice Huang, who was allegedly recruited as an intelligence asset by the Chinese government.

Read more

Latest News

Why CommonFloor’s $200M exit felt like a loss to co-founder Vikas Malpani

Vikas Malpani founded CommonFloor in 2007 with Sumit Jain and Lalit Mangal. In January 2016, Quikr announced it was merging the portal with QuikrHomes, its real estate business. The companies did not disclose the financial terms. Business Standard reported the deal was worth $200 million, while Malpani put the figure at more than $200 million in his LinkedIn post. All three co-founders left CommonFloor about a year after the acquisition. 

The acquisition came as investors were growing wary of startups burning through cash and Indian tech companies were buying smaller rivals to expand their businesses. Quikr struck two deals in 2015 and seven in 2016, according to VCCEdge data. CommonFloor gave it a bigger presence in online property listings, while another purchase that year, Grabhouse, helped it expand into managed rentals. Quikr also bought recruitment portal Hiree and folded it into QuikrJobs. 

Read more

Funding News

ValueQuest commits Rs 775 Cr to advance India’s defence, manufacturing push

ValueQuest Investment Advisors, a Mumbai-based investment manager, has made a total commitment of Rs 775 crore to three Indian businesses in defence technology, precision engineering, and power infrastructure.

The investment firm announced new investments in Sagar Defence Engineering and Rational Engineers and also added to its earlier investment in TASE Global. The Rs 775 crore is a portfolio commitment, not a single company’s fundraise.

Read more

Other News

IIT Madras unveils SEANAV, a real-time digital twin for autonomous ship navigation

Researchers at IIT Madras’s Department of Ocean Engineering have developed SEANAV, a Unity3D-based digital twin that lets autonomous maritime navigation systems be tested and trained in a realistic virtual ocean. It fuses LiDAR, radar and stereo-camera data while modelling noise, delays and poor visibility, and supports multi-agent AI that follows COLREGs in crowded waterways. A Meta Quest interface gives trainees a ship’s-bridge view. 

Calibrated on a 320-metre tanker, the platform could cut costly sea trials, improve port safety and lower emissions. Published in an ASME journal, future work targets digital twins of major Indian ports and certified VR pilot training."

Ultraviolette appoints ex-Royal Enfield marketer Abhijit Singh Brar as head of marketing

Ultraviolette has appointed Abhijit Singh Brar as Head of Marketing, tasking him with brand positioning, product launch strategy and demand generation as it widens its portfolio across India and overseas. Brar brings over two decades of experience, including more than eight years at Royal Enfield, where he built the marketing function from scratch and later led international marketing across Europe, the Americas, Australia and Southeast Asia.

He most recently held senior roles at Lodha, and earlier worked at Bacardi and Diageo. CEO Narayan Subramaniam said Brar's ability to build brands at scale will help the company reach new rider segments.

(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

item.title: Karnataka may subsidise GPU access for startups through AI hub
item.description: The state could offer support beyond the Centre’s IndiaAI Mission. It is also considering shared manufacturing space for small companies near Bengaluru.
item.content:encoded:
Karnataka is exploring whether it can subsidise access to graphics processing units (GPUs) for startups through its upcoming artificial intelligence hub at IIIT Bangalore. Karnataka IT and BT Secretary N. Manjula raised the possibility at a panel on how the state can support women in tech and entrepreneurship, after a founder building industrial smart cameras asked about cheaper computing power.

GPUs speed up AI model training and testing, and rental costs can limit how often early-stage startups experiment and refine their models.

When asked whether Karnataka could offer support on top of the Centre’s IndiaAI Mission, Manjula told YourStory after the panel, "We are open to looking at it.”

The central programme gives eligible startups access to subsidised cloud computing. Manjula gave no details on the budget, eligibility criteria, or the timeline for state support.

Rising hardware costs

IIIT Bangalore Director Debabrata Das said hardware costs, particularly for memory, had risen fourfold over the past year, with GPU prices seeing the next-biggest increase. He said the AI hub was looking at giving startups access to computing resources to test ideas and develop proofs of concept.

The Karnataka Cabinet approved the AI hub in September at an estimated cost of Rs 35 crore. The hub will offer AI training and startup support, and its planned AI Living Lab will provide computing infrastructure and a place to test applications. Das said more details were expected at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, which will be held from November 17 to 19.

Women-led startups account for 30–35% of ELEVATE winners

The panel provided women founders an opportunity to raise challenges they encounter at different stages of building and scaling their businesses.

Addressing the gathering, Manjula said, “Karnataka has consistently worked towards building a strong technology and startup ecosystem through policies and programmes that support the entire innovation journey, from skilling and research to incubation, funding and commercialisation. However, it is equally important for us to understand how these policies translate on the ground.

"This interaction is an opportunity to hear directly from women entrepreneurs, understand the challenges they face and identify areas where we can do better. The feedback shared today, particularly on access to funding, markets and infrastructure, will help us take these conversations forward and work towards more actionable solutions.”

Highlighting the state’s targeted interventions, she spoke about programmes such as Women@Work, WEscalate, BioWise and ELEVATE Shakti, which support women through skilling, incubation, mentoring, research exposure and financial assistance.

Under the latest edition of ELEVATE Shakti 2026, 63 women-led startups were selected, with grant support of Rs 23.19 crore committed. The broader ELEVATE Grant-in-Aid Programme has supported more than 400 women-led startups since 2017, with committed support of Rs 118.98 crore.

Women-led startups account for 30–35% of the winners of Karnataka’s ELEVATE programme each year, Manjula said. She added that the state had identified about 11 technology business incubators at academic institutions outside Bengaluru as part of its efforts to support founders beyond the city.

The cost of getting to proof of concept came up during the discussion. A biotech founder said she was using her savings to generate the early evidence she needed to qualify for a funding programme.

C-CAMP CEO Taslimarif Saiyed pointed to grants and incubators that can help founders at that stage and offered to discuss what support C-CAMP could provide.

Shared space for small manufacturers

Karnataka is also looking at a parcel of land roughly an hour from the Bengaluru airport where small companies could start manufacturing before they are able to afford premises of their own, Manjula said at the panel. She said discussions were at an early stage and raised the possibility of renting out space and setting up common facilities that companies in areas such as electronics and robotics could share.

Karnataka weighs how to deploy its Rs 300 Cr deeptech fund

A committee examining how Karnataka should deploy its Rs 300 crore deeptech fund of funds has drawn up recommendations and is expected to submit them to the government shortly, Manjula told YourStory. She gave no timeline for when investments could begin.

The Rs 300 crore figure matches the allocation for a fund of funds in Karnataka’s report on its LEAP initiative. Under this model, the state can channel public money through venture capital funds that invest in startups. That can help draw in private capital and leaves investment decisions to the fund managers.

item.title: Canonicus Capital raises Rs 192 Cr in its first close of Special Situations Fund
item.description: The firm will focus on deploying capital into selected opportunities across the National Capital Region (NCR), while continuing to build towards its Rs 500 crore target.
item.content:encoded:
Investment platform Canonicus Capital has announced the first close of its Special Situations Fund at Rs 192 crore, against a target corpus of Rs 500 crore.

Launched in 2025, the Special Situations Fund builds on the work of Canonicus Capital's Fund I through which it had raised and deployed Rs 311 crore. Together with Fund I, the first close takes Canonicus Capital's cumulative fundraising across its two funds to Rs 503 crore.

In a statement, the firm had said it will focus on deploying capital into selected opportunities across the National Capital Region (NCR), while continuing to build towards its Rs 500 crore target. 

The fund will focus on situations where disciplined capital allocation, strong governance and active execution can help unlock value.

The firm's international fundraising programme, which included roadshows across the Middle East and Singapore, was temporarily paused due to the West Asia conflict. As conditions improve, Canonicus Capital plans to resume its international investor outreach and build on the momentum of the fundraise.

“Raising commitments is only half the job. The Rs 192 crore first close gives us the flexibility to approach the next stage with discipline, and our focus now is deploying capital prudently and delivering returns for our investors. We are not passive capital providers; we are execution partners," Rajan Gupta, Managing Director, Canonicus Capital, said.

“NCR is a competitive market, with significant capital competing for a limited pool of quality projects. Yet several fundamentally sound businesses and projects remain overlooked due to governance gaps, capital constraints and execution challenges,” he added.

item.title: Jensen Huang exits Nvidia after 33 years; Kia India plans $2B investment in Andhra Pradesh
item.description: The transition comes at a critical juncture for Nvidia, whose chips have become the backbone of the global AI boom.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

It's the end of an era at Nvidia. Co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO after 33 years at the helm, following a turbulent week of controversy and board probes. More on Huang's sudden exit, the interim leadership and what comes next for the AI chip giant below.

After high-profile Indian public listings from portfolio giants like Swiggy and Amagi Media Labs, global investment firm Norwest has just closed its largest fund with a war chest of $4 billion. With its 18th fund, the 65-year-old firm is doubling down on its multi-stage strategy across India, the US, and Israel. The fund will back technology, healthcare and consumer businesses, from early-stage startups to companies preparing for public listings.

Closer home, CommonFloor co-founder Vikas Malpani reflects on why the company's $200 million acquisition by Quikr felt more like a loss than a victory. Rather than taking on advisory roles, he decided to start from scratch to launch social platform Leher before establishing Garvik AI. As the CEO of Garvik AI, he uses AI across sectors such as banking, edtech and real estate. 

Meanwhile, a year after Lenskart's IPO, co-founder and CEO Peyush Bansal says the company has yet to fulfil its original mission of making clear vision accessible to everyone. In a LinkedIn post, Bansal announced that Lenskart would stop charging extra for blue-light filtering lenses and offer prescription glasses to 100,000 children for a Rs 199 fitting fee. “What we have done is not enough,” he said.

Lastly, Mumbai-based investment manager ValueQuest Investment Advisors has made a total commitment of Rs 775 crore to three Indian businesses in defence technology, precision engineering, and power infrastructure. It has now backed Sagar Defence Engineering and Rational Engineers and also added to its earlier investment in TASE Global. The Rs 775 crore is a portfolio commitment, not a single company’s fundraise.

In today’s newsletter:

  • Nvidia's leadership shake-up and what comes next
  • Kia India plans $2B investment in Andhra Pradesh

Here’s your trivia for today: What name was given to the small robotic rover deployed onto the lunar surface by ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 lander in August 2023? (Scroll down for answer)

News

Jensen Huang exits Nvidia at a crucial time

Following a turbulent week of board probes and scandal, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, CEO, and board member effective immediately. His resignation brings his 33-year run at the helm to a sudden close as investors increasingly question the AI boom.

Longtime CFO Colette Kress is stepping in as interim chief executive while the board searches both internally and externally for a permanent successor. She joined Nvidia in 2013 after nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies including Cisco and Microsoft.

Key takeaways:

  • The transition comes at a critical juncture for Nvidia, whose chips have become the backbone of the global AI boom. Huang helped transform the company from a graphics-chip maker into one of the world's most influential technology businesses. His successor will have to sustain that momentum as competition intensifies and customers look to develop more of their own AI chips.
  • On November 8, Huang apologised in a company-published message for being unfaithful to his wife and pledged to co-operate with an independent board inquiry into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
  • Nvidia's CUDA software ecosystem has helped establish its dominance in AI computing, even as rivals develop alternatives.

Automobiles

Kia India plans $2B investment in Andhra Pradesh

Kia India has committed a combined investment of $2 billion, along with its supplier partners, to set up its second manufacturing facility in Andhra Pradesh. The company said the project would also help build India's manufacturing base, generate employment, and support the wider auto industry.

Key takeaways:

  • The factory will be located in Anantapur, the same district that houses Kia's current plant.
  • Kia India is targeting early 2030 for production to begin, with the plant carrying out stamping, welding, painting and assembly.
  • Kia and its suppliers will together occupy 465 acres on the new site. The company expects the facility to support roughly 12,000 jobs, both direct and indirect.

News & updates

  • Deeptech hub: Keralam wants to build its startup ecosystem and lead from the front, especially in deeptech and AI. At the inauguration of Huddle Global 2026, a beachside startup festival of the Keralam government, Chief Minister V D Satheesan said, “Our next task is to take Kerala's companies to the world. Kerala does not need the most startups. It must be the place where startups grow stronger.”
  • Funding: Investment platform Canonicus Capital has announced the first close of its Special Situations Fund at Rs 192 crore, against a target corpus of Rs 500 crore. Launched in 2025, the Special Situations Fund builds on the work of Canonicus Capital's Fund I through which it had raised and deployed Rs 311 crore.

What name was given to the small robotic rover deployed onto the lunar surface by ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 lander in August 2023?

Answer: Pragyan
