item.title: ValueQuest commits Rs 775 Cr to advance India’s defence, manufacturing push
item.description: The Mumbai-based investment manager is backing three businesses operating in the areas of defence tech, precision engineering, and power infrastructure: Sagar Defence Engineering, TASE Global, and Rational Engineers.
item.content:encoded:
ValueQuest Investment Advisors, a Mumbai-based investment manager, has made a total commitment of Rs 775 crore to three Indian businesses in defence technology, precision engineering, and power infrastructure.

The investment firm announced new investments in Sagar Defence Engineering and Rational Engineers and also added to its earlier investment in TASE Global. The Rs 775 crore is a portfolio commitment, not a single company’s fundraise.

Sagar Defence Engineering develops unmanned and autonomous systems for maritime and other defence applications. Rational Engineers makes specialised copper conductors and insulation products for power and distribution transformers. TASE Global operates in India and the United States, manufacturing precision components and assemblies for global original equipment manufacturers and Tier-I suppliers across medical technology, aerospace, defence and industrial markets.

ValueQuest says its private equity platform manages more than Rs 6,000 crore, including co-investments, and is building out SCALE Fund II.

The investment strategy reflects the wider shift in the manufacturing sector. Companies are diversifying supply chains and seeking to reduce dependence on overseas suppliers for strategically important technology and components. 

Ravi Dharamshi, Founder and Chief Investment Officer of ValueQuest, said, “The opportunity is not simply for India to manufacture more, but for Indian companies to develop the technology, capabilities and customer relationships to become globally competitive enterprises.”

Defence policy and procurement are helping drive this shift. The government reported that domestic defence production reached a record Rs 1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, with private firms accounting for 24%. Meanwhile, exports rose to Rs 38,424 crore.

The government is targeting annual production of Rs 3 lakh crore and exports of Rs 50,000 crore by 2029. It has also opened 25% of the defence research and development budget to industry, startups and academia.

Power infrastructure offers another source of demand. The National Electricity Plan envisages peak demand of 388 GW by 2032 and an increase in the transmission network from 5.09 lakh circuit kilometres in June 2026 to 6.48 lakh by 2032. This expansion should support demand for transformers and components, although actual orders will depend on project execution.

Aniket Dharamshi, Co-founder and Managing Partner, ValueQuest, said the firm was not rushing to deploy capital. “Our focus is not on the pace of capital deployment, but on identifying the right businesses,” he said.

Recently, ValueQuest’s Tristar Fund secured over Rs 2,100 crore in commitments within 15 months of its first close, exceeding its original target and greenshoe.

item.title: Norwest closes $4B fund to back AI, healthcare and financial infra
item.description: Norwest’s $4 billion fund signals a long-term bet on AI, healthcare and technology, as the investment firm looks to back businesses across markets, stages and sectors.
item.content:encoded:
Norwest, an investment firm focused on venture capital and growth equity, has closed a $4 billion fund, Norwest 18, the largest in its 65-year history. It will back companies in technology, healthcare and consumer markets across the US, India and Israel, from early-stage ventures to established businesses.

Founded in 1961, Norwest says it has invested in more than 750 companies and currently works with over 275 portfolio businesses. Its Indian investments include OfBusiness and Swiggy, and it has a Mumbai office. The firm notes its multi-stage approach is intended to support companies as they move from early development to expansion.

Norwest 18 follows Norwest 17, launched in April 2024. Since then, the firm says it has made more than 87 investments and worked with over 30 portfolio companies to achieve liquidity events, when investors can realise value from a holding. These include stock market listings by Amagi Media Labs and Swiggy, and acquisitions of businesses including Qualified by Salesforce and Veza by ServiceNow.

The firm believes its role extends beyond providing capital, particularly as businesses face more complicated growth decisions. Senior Managing Partner Jeff Crowe said companies are staying private for longer, expanding across markets and navigating increasingly complex decisions involving technology, talent and growth. 

“Capital is only one part of what they need,” he said, emphasising the importance of long-term support, industry experience and networks.

Norwest expects AI to create opportunities across its established sectors and newer areas, including financial infrastructure, physical and voice AI, cybersecurity for AI agents, industrial technology, aerospace and healthcare. Norwest cites Beltic, Rain and Stablecore in payments and digital-currency infrastructure, and LlamaIndex and Generalist AI in intelligent systems.

The strategy comes as Indian technology investment becomes more concentrated. AI startups in the country raised $1.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $677 million a year earlier, but funding rounds fell 43%. Four large deals accounted for 72% of the total, indicating that capital is flowing disproportionately to infrastructure and model developers, while application businesses struggle to convert interest into paying customers.

Recent Indian fundraises show activity across related sectors. Bengaluru-based Even Healthcare raised $50 million in October from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave to expand its managed-care and hospital operations, while wealth technology startup PowerUp Money raised $10 million in November, led by Flourish Ventures, to develop AI-enabled wealth management.

Policy is also shaping the market. The IndiaAI Mission has expanded shared computing capacity to more than 45,000 graphics processing units, and selected 20 proposals for locally developed foundation AI models. In July, the Cabinet approved Semicon 2.0, with a Rs 1.275 trillion budget for semiconductor design and manufacturing.

Norwest is also strengthening support beyond funding by doubling its Senior Advisor Network, adding operating executives and launching the Norwest Operator Collective and Norwest Kinetic. 

Managing Partner Jon Kossow said Norwest’s investment approach was built around maintaining long-term relationships with businesses as their requirements evolve. Its multi-stage strategy allows the firm to “meet companies where they are” and continue supporting them as they grow, he said.

item.title: ‘What we have done is not enough’: Lenskart CEO a year after IPO
item.description: One year after Lenskart’s public listing, CEO Peyush Bansal scrapped blue-light lens upsells and pledged free glasses to 100,000 children to target India’s widespread vision accessibility crisis.
item.content:encoded:
One year after debuting as a public enterprise, optical retail group Lenskart has chosen to evaluate its corporate milestone through the lens of unresolved societal challenges. 

In an open statement marking the anniversary of its initial public offering, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Peyush Bansal acknowledged that despite expanding access to affordable eyewear across India, the core objective of rendering clear vision a universal reality remains unfinished. 

The company announced structural operational changes aimed at reducing financial barriers for essential eye care. 

“We built a ten thousand crore company. The one thing we started it for is still unsolved,” Bansal stated.

Lenskart was established with an ambition to enable one billion people to see clearly, beginning with targeted efforts across India. The organisation currently supplies approximately 32 million eyewear units annually in India and aims to increase output to 100 million units in its next phase of expansion. 

Over several years, the enterprise invested heavily in localised manufacturing capabilities to lower production costs for sophisticated optical products. These investments included developing domestic facilities for progressive lenses, which are multifocal lenses that allow smooth visual transitions across varying distances without visible dividing lines. 

The firm also developed local capacity for break-resistant rimless frames and complete prescription pairs priced at Rs 500. Corporate leadership maintains that manufacturing scale serves as an operational tool to solve systemic health issues.

Addressing the rapid digitalisation of daily life in India, where nearly one billion citizens regularly engage with screens, Lenskart announced the immediate removal of extra fees for blue-light filtering coatings. Blue-light filtering lenses contain specialised protective coatings designed to minimise digital glare and eye fatigue caused by prolonged screen exposure. Under the new policy, these protective coatings will come as standard on all prescription eyewear sold by the company in India without additional charges.

Furthermore, the retailer is directing resources toward childhood vision health to combat undetected myopia, a medical term for short-sightedness that hinders clear distance vision and can impair learning outcomes. To mark National Children’s Day on, Lenskart will provide free prescription glasses featuring blue-light filtering lenses to the first 100,000 child visitors across its Indian stores, requiring families to pay only a Rs 199 fitting fee.

In retail optics, specialised lens treatments typically serve as high-margin add-ons. By making screen-ready lenses standard and funding large-scale paediatric eye health initiatives, Lenskart is likely absorbing short-term margin trade-offs in pursuit of broader consumer trust and long-term brand equity. 

“Purpose and profit are not a trade-off. In the short term, the right thing for the customer rarely looks like the obvious decision. In the long term, it has worked out every single time,” Bansal noted.

item.title: Kia India to invest $2B in second plant in Andhra Pradesh
item.description: Spread across a combined 465 acres for Kia and its suppliers, the new facility is expected to generate around 12,000 direct and indirect job opportunities.
item.content:encoded:
Kia India has committed a combined investment of $2 billion, along with its supplier partners, to set up its second manufacturing facility in Andhra Pradesh.

The carmaker signed a memorandum of understanding with the state government to formalise the plan.

The factory will be located in Anantapur, the same district that houses Kia's current plant. It will add 2 lakh units of annual manufacturing capacity, taking Kia India’s combined capacity across both plants to over 6 lakh units a year.

Kia India is targeting early 2030 for production to begin, with the plant carrying out stamping, welding, painting and assembly. This plant will manufacture new models across ICE and EV powertrains, the company said in a statement.

Kia and its suppliers will together occupy 465 acres on the new site. The company expects the facility to support roughly 12,000 jobs, both direct and indirect.

In comparison, the first plant, across 945 acres, employs 24,237 people through direct and indirect roles. Set up with an initial investment of $2.9 billion, the facility builds the Seltos, Syros, Sonet, Carens, Carens Clavis, Carnival and Sorento models, spanning ICE, EV, CNG and hybrid versions.

Gwanggu Lee, Managing Director and CEO, Kia India, said, “India is central to Kia’s long-term growth ambitions, and the trust our customers have placed in us since we began operations in Anantapur has been instrumental in our journey."

He continued, "Our second manufacturing plant marks a significant new chapter, strengthening our ability to respond to customer demand with greater speed and flexibility, while supporting the introduction of new models across ICE and EV powertrains.

"As we enter our next phase of growth, we remain committed to contributing to India’s automotive ecosystem and building on the strong foundation we have created here. This will further expand our Made-in-India footprint, strengthening our ability to serve both domestic and overseas markets.”

Kia said the project would also help build India's manufacturing base, generate employment, and support the wider auto industry.

item.title: Why CommonFloor’s $200M exit felt like a loss to co-founder Vikas Malpani
item.description: A decade after Quikr bought the real estate portal, Malpani reflects on leaving the startup he had spent years building and why he chose to start again.
item.content:encoded:
Vikas Malpani thought he would feel like he had won when Quikr bought CommonFloor in 2016. He had spent several years co-building the startup, which began as a tool for apartment communities and grew into a property portal that reached millions of users. The company had been the focus of his working life. After the acquisition, Malpani missed the structure the company had given him. “I expected to feel like I had won. I felt like something had ended,” he wrote in a LinkedIn post⁠.

The deal that brought CommonFloor into Quikr

Malpani founded CommonFloor in 2007 with Sumit Jain and Lalit Mangal. In January 2016, Quikr announced it was merging the portal with QuikrHomes, its real estate business. The companies did not disclose the financial terms. Business Standard reported the deal was worth $200 million, while Malpani put the figure at more than $200 million in his LinkedIn post. All three co-founders left CommonFloor about a year after the acquisition. 

The acquisition came as investors were growing wary of startups burning through cash and Indian tech companies were buying smaller rivals to expand their businesses. Quikr struck two deals in 2015 and seven in 2016, according to VCCEdge data. CommonFloor gave it a bigger presence in online property listings, while another purchase that year, Grabhouse, helped it expand into managed rentals. Quikr also bought recruitment portal Hiree and folded it into QuikrJobs. 

Starting over after CommonFloor

In an essay on his website, Malpani said he could have stayed in real estate, become a full-time investor or taken an advisory role. He went back to building companies, co-founding Leher, a social platform for live audio and video. The move took him into a business with very different economics from a property portal. Learning how that business worked, he wrote, came more easily than letting go of the identity he had built around CommonFloor. He also had to question whether the instincts he had developed there still applied. 

Malpani is now co-founder and CEO of Garvik AI, which builds AI tools for businesses. Its ReBillion.ai platform helps employees find information across their company and lets businesses set up AI assistants. Malpani says the company has deployed those tools in banking, manufacturing, education technology and real estate. That last sector brings him back to a market he knows well, this time selling software to businesses after spending years building a portal for people looking for homes.

item.title: Kutlerri.ai raises $4M to help US restaurants grow revenue and cut costs using AI agents
item.description: Founded by former HighRadius executives Kiran Rana and Payal Tripathy, Kutlerri.ai charges restaurants a percentage of the revenue its AI agents generate or the costs they save.
item.content:encoded:
Houston and Bhubaneswar-based Kutlerri.ai has raised $4 million from Houston-based Narahari Investments to scale its AI agents that help restaurants increase revenue and reduce operating costs.

Founded in December 2025 by former HighRadius executives Kiran Rana and Payal Tripathy, the startup develops AI agents that handle specific revenue and cost-related tasks for restaurants. Unlike conventional software subscriptions, Kutlerri.ai charges operators based on the revenue generated or costs saved by its agents.

The company currently serves restaurants in the US and has more than 10 signed customers. Its product and engineering team is based in Bhubaneswar, Odisha; it also has an office in Houston, Texas. The core founding team includes Ankit Narain and Rishabh Srivastav.

The funding will help scale its first commercial product, the AI Catering Sales Agent, bring three agents currently in beta to market, and develop a mobile-first self-service app.

Addressing restaurant profitability

According to the National Restaurant Association's 2026 State of the Restaurant Industry report, US restaurant and foodservice sales are projected to reach $1.55 trillion in 2026, although 42% of operators surveyed reported that they did not make a profit in 2025.

The association also noted in July 2026 that rising costs continued to put pressure on restaurant profitability. Even before the post-pandemic increase in costs, a typical restaurant retained only about five cents of every dollar earned.

With margins this narrow, even small improvements can make a difference. Kutlerri.ai focuses on increasing revenue and reducing costs through AI agents that take on tasks restaurants may not have dedicated staff to manage.

Restaurants already use software for point-of-sale operations, kitchen displays, inventory, online ordering, payroll, and accounting. However, these systems primarily record information rather than act on it.

For instance, catering enquiries may go unanswered, or delivery advertisements may continue running without producing results. Addressing such problems generally requires dedicated staff, which many independent restaurants cannot afford.

Kutlerri.ai’s agents are designed to handle these tasks. Its revenue agents work on catering, third-party delivery, and online ordering, while its cost agents focus on delivery advertising, food and labour costs, daily preparation, and waste.

Restaurants can use the agents through a fully managed service or, once launched, a mobile-first self-service app. In both models, Kutlerri.ai charges a percentage of the additional revenue generated or costs saved. If an agent does not deliver measurable results, the restaurant does not pay.

Catering agent generates $450,000 for RASA

Kutlerri.ai's first commercial product focuses on catering sales.

According to MONKEY's State of Catering 2026 report, 60% of catering orders came from just 5% of customers. The findings were based on transactional data from more than 8,000 restaurant locations and two million catering orders.

The figures highlight the importance of attracting new catering customers and reconnecting with previous ones, particularly for restaurants without dedicated sales teams.

The AI Catering Sales Agent identifies potential catering customers within a 30-mile radius of a restaurant. It contacts businesses through email, text messages, and phone calls, reconnects with inactive customers, responds to incoming calls, chats, and emails, and closes orders. Restaurant operators approve decisions and retain their customer relationships.

Kutlerri.ai developed the agent with RASA, a five-location fast-casual restaurant group in the Washington, DC, area. The two companies worked together to develop the product around RASA’s catering sales requirements, with the restaurant group paying for the service throughout the development period.

According to Kutlerri.ai, the agent generated $450,000 in new catering revenue for RASA over 10 months, more than 10X the amount the restaurant group paid for the service, without requiring additional hires.

The catering agent is now live with operators in most major US cities, the company said.

From HighRadius to restaurant operations

Rana, CEO, and Tripathy, COO, previously worked at HighRadius, where business functions had clear ownership of financial performance.

Their interest in the restaurant sector began after observing the operations of a restaurant run by someone close to them. While the restaurant used several systems to track performance, there was no dedicated person to act on the information.

The founders subsequently spoke with other operators, including fast-casual restaurants and multi-location groups generating around $3 million annually.

They found similar challenges: scattered data, delayed identification of problems, decisions based on judgement rather than data, and margins that had remained unchanged for years.

These observations led them to build Kutlerri.ai around AI agents that could take responsibility for specific revenue and cost-related functions.

Expansion plans

Kutlerri.ai’s product & engineering, marketing, business development and customer success teams operate from India, with each function responsible for outcomes linked to restaurant profitability.

The company currently has one commercially available agent, three agents in beta testing inside restaurants, and two more under development.

It plans to expand its strategy, marketing, customer success and engineering teams as it develops and launches these products.

While Kutlerri.ai currently focuses on US restaurants, it is open to expanding into India and other markets in the future. As the company continues to grow, explore career opportunities with the team careers@kutlerri.ai.
